ctx.x: Well you mentioned Pierron's band and what type of music they play. I forgot to mention it was in the year about 1915. I think Pierron then used mostly string instruments. And he played regular conventional ragtime like I had right on records that was of that date of error. There's some things I'd like to tell you that I may have forgotten to mention. items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: The interviewee (Nick La Rocca) is reading a letter from J.C. Avady. The letter mentions 'Rags' in the context of Harry James hiring a band consisting of 'Nunes, Rags, and Stein'. ctx.x: Their champion was a colored man. Let's say a colored man has his rightful place in any music. Why not the white man to eulogize another man that hasn't created anything because of his color? That must be his music. But although Elvin Presley went on to hikes while the other guy stayed there, if you listen to his style, he couldn't have been original because he changed four or five different times. This is a letter. Headed Paris, December 16, 1956. Dear Mr. LaRocca, The very long trip I have done through the world is at its end. I am just arrived from Melbourne this morning with a great regret not to have been in New Orleans for meeting you. But fate is blind and can offer me a very next opportunity to go to the States for another film. I suppose you have well received my letter dated November the 11th that I have sent you from Calcutta. If you don't, I will mail you a copy. The 1956 Olympic Games were very…

Cafe what wonderful music the Tom Brown Band had, and he wired us an offer to play at his place. The price was right, I'm sorry, to play at his place, period. The price was right and we accepted the job, period. That is how this dance team helped give our music a start, period. They were the first ones to tell Chicago about the Browns Dixieland Band, period. items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-06-14
items.q: The first man to bring this down on me was Marshall Steins. Probably other men had written about it. But he is the one over here that went and got the Guggenheimer Foundation.

ctx.x: This is a Negro who had never been recognized, invented by Alan Lomax. With a few jugs of wine and a couple of needles, furnished by the doctors in New Orleans. He was a set up and tell the history of jazz. A Negro who had never been recognized. Saw what the world broke. Nobody ever listened to him, but Alan Lomax happened to be one of the clique. That is Marshall Starnes, I can name him, for I don't have the list of them. They got a whole bunch of them. They live by piracy and lies. That's all they ever did in…

Well, I don't really think I can, Mr. Rocker. I think that I think I've covered everything. After all, I'm one of those people that just like listening to jazz music. I haven't any sort of first-hand knowledge of what really went on. I wasn't around. I wasn't even born when the first records were made, when jazz was created.
